title: Choose the load balancer from the traffic
copy: ALB: understand HTTP
Use Layer 7 request routing for web applications, APIs, HTTP/2 and WebSockets. Rules select application target groups.
NLB: handle transport flows
Use high-throughput, low-latency transport load balancing and static zonal addresses. Choose compatible TCP, TLS or UDP listeners.
GWLB: insert inspection
Distribute IP traffic to virtual appliances, such as firewalls, IDS/IPS and deep packet inspection systems.
Legacy context
Classic Load Balancer supports HTTP, HTTPS, TCP and SSL. Prefer a modern type for new architectures.
Remember: Start with protocol, routing and security requirements; performance alone does not choose the service.

title: Listener, rule, target group: three decisions
copy: Listener: accept traffic
Choose the client-facing protocol and port, such as HTTPS on 443. This does not define the application's backend port.
Rule: choose an action
ALB evaluates rules from lowest numeric priority upward, then uses the default rule. Forward, redirect or return a fixed response.
Target group: reach the application
Define eligible targets, backend protocol and port, health checks and supported routing attributes.
Keep the boundaries clear
One ALB can serve several applications through different target groups. A healthy load balancer does not prove that every backend is ready.
Remember: The listener accepts; the rule decides; the target group delivers.
layout: Three offset glossy conceptual cards, one detailed callout beneath; do not draw exact topology.

title: Public entry point, private application
copy: Internet-facing
Public addresses accept internet traffic when routing and security permit. Targets can remain on private addresses.
Internal
Private addresses serve reachable private clients through the VPC, peering, VPN or Direct Connect, subject to routing and controls.
Reachability still matters
DNS resolution alone is insufficient. Check subnet routes, address families, security groups and network ACLs.
Design for resilience
Enable suitable Availability Zones and register capacity in them. An internal load balancer is not an authorization system.
Remember: Load balancer scheme controls reachability; identity and network policy control access.

title: Cross-zone balancing changes the target pool
copy: Cross-zone enabled
A load balancer node can send traffic to eligible healthy targets across enabled zones. Uneven zonal capacity is easier to share.
Cross-zone disabled
A node uses targets in its own zone. Each zone needs enough healthy capacity for the traffic that arrives there.
Defaults and controls
ALB is enabled at the load balancer level; eligible target groups can disable it. NLB and GWLB default to disabled. CLB defaults depend on creation method.
Availability and cost
Cross-zone routing is separate from client DNS routing. Check current inter-AZ transfer charges and capacity needs for the selected service.
Remember: Sharing targets across zones does not remove the need to survive a zone failure.

title: Health checks measure application readiness
copy: Choose a meaningful probe
Configure the target-group protocol, port, path, success matcher, interval and thresholds. A listening socket may still hide a broken application.
Read the reason code
Separate timeout, response-code mismatch, failed health check and unused target states before changing infrastructure.
Avoid a shared outage cascade
A probe that fails whenever a shared dependency fails can remove every target at once. Design readiness checks deliberately.
Understand fail-open
If all ALB targets are unhealthy across enabled zones, traffic can be sent to all of them. Unhealthy is not a guaranteed traffic block.
Remember: Health checks guide routing; they do not repair applications or replace security controls.
layout: Four generous cards with glossy stethoscope, code badge, dependency and amber warning illustrations.

title: ALB routes by the request's meaning
copy: Match the request
Conditions include host, path, HTTP headers, request method, query strings and source IP. Order specific rules before broad matches.
Choose the response
Forward to target groups, redirect HTTP to HTTPS, or return a fixed response. The default rule handles unmatched requests.
Use the protocol features
ALB supports HTTP/2 and WebSocket upgrades. After an upgrade, messages use the established connection to the selected target.
Example decision
Requests for shop.example.com and /checkout can reach the checkout service; /catalog can reach another group without another public ALB.
Remember: Routing identifies the destination; it does not grant permission to use that destination.

title: ALB targets: instances, IPs and functions
copy: Instance or IP targets
Instance registration uses the instance's primary private address. IP targets support eligible private ranges and reachable hybrid workloads; public IP targets are not supported.
Container port mapping
ECS on EC2 with bridge networking can map identical container ports to different host ports. ECS registers the appropriate target ports.
Fargate and awsvpc
Tasks have their own network interfaces and private addresses. Use IP target groups rather than registering the host instance.
Lambda target
ALB translates an HTTP request into a JSON event and converts the function response back to HTTP. Follow the ALB event and response contract.
Remember: Choose the target type to match what actually receives the traffic.
layout: Four glossary panels with glossy server, container stack, interface and function illustrations; no invented port labels.

title: TLS termination: identify both connections
copy: Client to ALB
An HTTPS listener needs a server certificate and security policy. SNI lets one listener select among certificates for different hostnames.
ALB to target
Choose HTTP or HTTPS independently. HTTPS encrypts the backend leg; ALB does not validate the target certificate.
Client certificates
ALB mTLS verify authenticates client certificates against a trust store. In mTLS passthrough mode, certificate details go to the application in HTTP headers.
Different meaning of passthrough
NLB with a TCP listener can pass encrypted TLS bytes to the target for end-to-end termination. ALB mTLS passthrough still terminates TLS at ALB.
Remember: Encryption, server identity and client identity are three separate requirements.
layout: Two illuminated lock sculptures above four readable explanation cards; conceptual not precise topology.

title: Authenticate users, then authorize actions
copy: Offload sign-in
ALB HTTPS listener authentication supports OIDC providers or Amazon Cognito user pools. Cognito can federate corporate or social identities.
Preserve the login journey
Configure callback URLs, client credentials, scopes and connectivity to the identity provider. An internal ALB may still need outbound access to IdP endpoints.
Protect the backend
Validate the ALB-signed claims and expected signer before trusting identity headers. Prevent clients from bypassing the ALB.
Application authorization remains
A valid login does not prove permission to read every record or perform every action. Enforce resource-level authorization in the application.
Remember: Authentication establishes who the user is; authorization decides what the user may do.

title: Choose how ALB distributes requests
copy: Round robin
Default sequential distribution across healthy targets; useful when requests and target capabilities are similar.
Least outstanding requests
Prefers targets with fewer in-progress requests. Useful when request duration or processing capability varies.
Weighted random
Random distribution with optional Automatic Target Weights anomaly mitigation. It cannot be combined with stickiness or slow start.
Stickiness and warm-up
Duration-based or application cookies keep a client on a target but can create imbalance. Slow start gradually increases a new target's share; use a compatible algorithm.
Remember: Target selection is different from weighted forwarding between target groups.
layout: Four large polished concept tiles with evenly sized readable text; use no data chart.

title: Drain connections before removing capacity
copy: Deregister safely
A deregistering target enters draining. Stop assigning new work and allow in-flight requests to finish within the configured delay.
Know the timer
For ALB instance and IP targets, deregistration delay defaults to 300 seconds and can be configured from 0 to 3600 seconds.
Coordinate the application
Align container or process shutdown grace, long requests and connection handling. Terminating the process early can still break requests.
Roll out in stages
Start replacement capacity, wait for readiness, shift traffic, drain old targets and then terminate. Health and rollback checks belong in the deployment.
Remember: Deregistration delay is a chance to finish work, not a guarantee that every request survives.
layout: Four staggered glossy lifecycle cards; no precise flowchart.

title: Weighted target groups enable controlled releases
copy: Split new requests
An ALB forward action assigns relative weights to target groups. A 90:10 split is an intended distribution, not an exact small-sample guarantee.
Account for stickiness
Group-level stickiness can keep a client in the selected group. Existing sessions may not immediately follow a changed weight.
Do not assume automatic failover
If a weighted group is empty or unhealthy, ALB does not automatically move its assigned traffic to another healthy group.
Make rollback practical
Observe errors, latency and business outcomes. Restore weights when needed; schema and data compatibility require their own rollback plan.
Remember: Weighted forwarding controls traffic share; deployment safety requires health signals and compatible state.
layout: Two glossy release-version pedestals, amber control dial and four concise explanatory cards, no numeric chart.

title: NLB: choose transport and TLS behavior
copy: Layer 4 transport listeners
TCP, TLS, UDP and TCP_UDP address common workloads. QUIC and TCP_QUIC are also supported with specific configuration restrictions.
Terminate or pass through
A TLS listener terminates client TLS and needs a certificate. A TCP listener on 443 can carry encrypted TLS unchanged to the application.
Select compatible targets
Targets: instances, private IPs from eligible ranges, or ALB. Public IP targets are unsupported. Match listener and target protocols; an ALB target requires TCP.
Avoid false guarantees
NLB is designed for demanding transport workloads. Fixed latency comparisons and promises of unlimited connections are not architecture guarantees.
Remember: Choose who terminates TLS before choosing the listener protocol.
layout: Large glossy transport connector and lock comparison, four text cards with ample space.

title: NLB addresses, DNS and client identity
copy: Static zonal addresses
NLB provides a static address per enabled zone. Internet-facing IPv4 deployments can use an Elastic IP per zone for allowlists.
Regional or zonal DNS
The regional name can return healthy node addresses across zones. A zonal DNS name identifies a specific zone's node; the application must manage its resilience.
Client identity at the target
Client IP preservation depends on protocol and target settings. Proxy Protocol v2 can carry connection metadata when the application understands it.
Plan the whole path
DNS zonal affinity influences client-to-NLB selection; cross-zone balancing influences NLB-to-target selection. They solve different parts of locality.
Remember: A fixed address is zonal; resilient clients must handle multiple zones.
layout: Glossy address plaque, DNS compass and identity envelope in three rich illustrations with explanatory blocks.

title: NLB keeps flows together and checks health
copy: Flow-based selection
NLB selects a target using flow information: protocol, source and destination addresses and ports; TCP also uses the sequence number. An established flow stays with that target.
Probe the real service
Active checks can use TCP, HTTP or HTTPS. UDP services need a suitable non-UDP health endpoint that reflects the UDP application's health.
Know failure behavior
Unhealthy zonal capacity can cause zonal addresses to leave DNS. If all targets fail, NLB can fail open; empty target groups can also trigger fail-open.
Connection handling matters
Idle timeouts, target termination and unhealthy-target behavior affect existing flows. More healthy targets do not transparently migrate a live TCP connection.
Remember: Balancing connections does not mean balancing every application message.
layout: Glossy bundled cable analogy and pulse probe; four panels, no hash calculation diagram.

title: PrivateLink and NLB-to-ALB composition
copy: Publish a private service
An endpoint service backed by NLB lets consumers connect through interface endpoints. Configure allowed principals and acceptance requirements.
Keep service boundaries narrow
PrivateLink exposes the service; it does not create full network peering. Provider and consumer routing and policies still matter.
Combine transport and HTTP features
An NLB can use an ALB as its target, combining static entry addresses or PrivateLink with ALB HTTP routing.
Respect composition constraints
The NLB and ALB must share the VPC and account. Use an ALB target group with TCP and a port matching an ALB listener; configure health checks.
Remember: Combine load balancers only when the requirements justify the extra layer, cost and failure surface.

title: GWLB inserts an appliance inspection service
copy: Inspect IP traffic at Layer 3
GWLB combines transparent network-gateway behavior with load distribution across virtual firewalls, IDS/IPS or other network appliances.
Use compatible appliances
The appliance fleet exchanges traffic with GWLB using GENEVE encapsulation on UDP port 6081. Targets can be instances or eligible private IP addresses.
Connect through endpoints
Gateway Load Balancer endpoints carry traffic between the consumer VPC and inspection service. GWLB resides with the appliances in the provider VPC.
Routing is part of the design
Route tables must steer the intended traffic through inspection and support the return path. Deploying an endpoint alone does not inspect all traffic.
Remember: GWLB distributes inspection traffic; the appliance supplies the security policy.
layout: Glossy magnifying shield, packet capsule and appliance fleet illustration with readable four blocks; avoid precise routes.

title: GWLB flow affinity protects stateful inspection
copy: Keep the flow consistent
The default 5-tuple uses source and destination addresses, ports and protocol. Configurable 3-tuple or 2-tuple stickiness supports specific appliance requirements.
Preserve symmetry
A stateful appliance must see the relevant forward and return traffic. Validate routing and appliance mode when integrating other network services.
Plan appliance failure
Health checks identify available targets, but reassignment of existing flows depends on configured failover behavior. A new appliance may lack the old session state.
Scale with evidence
Monitor appliance capacity, health and flow behavior. Test draining, failure and recovery under realistic traffic before relying on the design.
Remember: Healthy replacement capacity does not automatically preserve an existing inspection session.
layout: Glossy paired packet ribbons around shield, conceptual session ledger, four explanatory panels.

title: Secure both the entry point and the target
copy: ALB application protection
AWS WAF can filter supported HTTP requests at ALB. Security groups control network access; WAF and security groups solve different problems.
NLB security groups
Associate a security group when creating the NLB if needed. An NLB created without any cannot have security groups added later; protocol-specific restrictions apply.
Target access and health checks
Where supported, reference the load balancer security group in the target's security group rules on application and health-check ports. Check outbound rules and stateless NACL return traffic.
Trust proxy headers carefully
ALB provides X-Forwarded-For, X-Forwarded-Proto and X-Forwarded-Port. Trust only the secured proxy chain; arbitrary incoming header values are not proof of identity.
Remember: Prevent direct target bypass and evaluate identity separately from network reachability.
layout: Layered glossy shield illustration surrounded by four readable panels; do not depict exact topology.

title: Diagnose ingress with evidence
copy: Start with target health
Read the target state and reason code. Verify the application listener, probe path, expected response, security groups, routes and network ACLs.
Separate error sources
Compare load-balancer errors with target errors. A client-facing failure may originate before a target is reached or inside the application.
Correlate metrics and logs
Use healthy-target counts, response time, request volume and error metrics. ALB access logs record request details; traditional delivery uses S3, with newer logging integrations also available.
Follow the request
Check TLS negotiation, rule selection, target registration, application logs and dependencies. Verify the corrected path rather than changing every layer at once.
Remember: A green load-balancer resource is not evidence that the user's request succeeds.
layout: Glossy magnifier, telemetry console illustration without fabricated exact console UI, four explanation blocks.

title: Choose ingress for the actual requirement
copy: Many HTTP services, one entry point
Choose ALB for host or path routing, HTTP-aware controls and supported web protocols.
Stable addresses plus HTTP routing
Consider NLB targeting ALB when static zonal entry addresses or PrivateLink must coexist with ALB features.
Encrypted transport to the application
Use a compatible NLB TCP listener when the target must terminate the client's TLS connection.
Transparent appliance inspection
Use GWLB for an eligible third-party appliance fleet; preserve flow consistency and required routing.
Check the tradeoffs
Include capacity, quotas, transfer, logging, public IPv4 and load-balancer usage costs. Compare current pricing rather than memorizing old free-tier or latency claims.
Remember: Select the simplest design that satisfies protocol, security, availability and operating requirements.
layout: Four glossy scenario vignettes plus small cost lens; each vignette has full readable explanation.

title: Classic Load Balancer: understand the legacy
copy: Protocols and certificates
CLB supports HTTP, HTTPS, TCP and SSL. It does not support SNI. One certificate can cover multiple SAN names; changing those names requires a certificate update, or use separate load balancers.
TLS at the instance
A TCP listener can pass encrypted bytes to the instance, where the application can implement mTLS. Modern ALB also supports client-certificate authentication.
Health and request distribution
CLB health checks support TCP, SSL, HTTP or HTTPS. HTTP/HTTPS request routing uses least outstanding requests; TCP uses round robin. Cookie stickiness can preserve sessions but create imbalance.
Cross-zone and migration
Cross-zone defaults differ by creation method. Compare modern ALB or NLB features, migrate deliberately and test certificates, health checks, sessions and rollback.
Remember: Legacy knowledge explains existing systems; choose current service capabilities for new designs.

title: AWS Load Balancer Controller connects Kubernetes to ELB
copy: Reconcile declared intent
The controller watches Kubernetes resources and creates or updates AWS load-balancing resources to match. Give it appropriate IAM permissions and subnet discovery configuration.
Choose the Kubernetes resource
An Ingress managed by the controller provisions ALB for HTTP routing. A Service of type LoadBalancer managed by it provisions NLB for transport traffic.
Choose the target mode
Instance mode reaches node ports; IP mode registers pod addresses. Fargate pods require IP targets. Keep routing, security groups and pod readiness aligned.
Avoid competing owners
Use the correct ingress class or loadBalancerClass. EKS Auto Mode has its own integrated load-balancing capabilities; distinguish the chosen controller and its configuration.
Remember: Kubernetes declares the desired exposure; the controller reconciles the AWS resources.
layout: Glossy declarative blueprint and controller gears alongside two large service cards. Conceptual illustrations, no exact topology.

title: Zonal locality: balance resilience and transfer cost
copy: Know the cross-zone cost difference
ALB and CLB do not add regional transfer charges for their cross-zone load balancing. NLB and GWLB cross-zone traffic can incur inter-AZ transfer charges.
Keep each hop in view
Client-to-load-balancer traffic, load-balancer-to-target traffic and later application calls are separate hops. An exempt hop does not make the entire request path free.
Use locality deliberately
NLB zonal DNS or supported Route 53 Resolver zonal-affinity policies influence which node clients reach. Disable cross-zone routing only with sufficient capacity in every serving zone.
Budget for the complete service
Include load-balancer usage or capacity charges, applicable endpoints, public IPv4, logging and transfer. Use current regional pricing and validate failure behavior.
Remember: Locality saves cost only when it preserves the availability and capacity the workload needs.
